title: Billie Pierce and De De Pierce Interview, 1959-04-02

pages.label: 001_Billie Pierce and De De Pierce Interview, 1959-04-02 Part 1

blocks.x: It's all set going. You might give your names first so we'll have that on the tape. Do you want to start, Billy? Tell us, give your name first and then your family before you were married.

Oh, yeah. Oh, before I was married, I was a good son. Now since I got married, I'm named Willie Madison Pierce, but I still use that good son over there too right on. And I have three sisters living. It was seven of us, but just only three living now. Which ones are living now? Well, Sadie, she is living. She's the oldest one living. Is she still in New York? No, Sadie's in Detroit. Oh, Detroit. I don't even know. And then Edna, she's next to Sadie. She's in Florida. And I had also my baby sister, she was in Florida. Now just where were you born?
Yeah, I was born in Florida. Was that Pensacola? I was born in Mariana, Florida. Oh, Mariana.
Mariana, Florida. Also...
What was the date? When was your birthday?
My birthday, it was on the 8th of June. It was on the Tuesday when my birthday fell last year. What year were you born? I was born in 1907. 1907.

D.D., you might tell a little bit when you were... What was your birth date, how we think of it, so we'll be sure to get that. February 18th, 1904. 1904. Where were you born? New Orleans, right here. Do you remember the street? I mean, you wouldn't remember, but I mean they told you. Which street you...
St. Anne... No, let me get straight. I think it's Rushbrave. Rushbrave... What was it called? Old Indian Market.
Oh, yes.
Back there.
Back there.
Yeah, that's near Iberville somewhere in the city.
Were your folks musical?
No, none in the family.
Your father or mother didn't play or sing anything much? No, they played at all.

None of them did any musical, not at all. I just, you know, I liked it by hearing bands playing, you know. Yeah. I'd be in the take and take... In other words, I had a cousin, she was trying to play in the girl band. Her name was Leliska at the time. I was about seventeen then at the time. And she gave me an old trumpet and I just began to play by ear. And finally, I heard of a teacher, which was Kid Rene, he's also deceased.
Oh, yes.

Yeah. And I had my first few lessons from him. And then I left him and went and learnt more my reading, like the music part, from my shallow knee. He was an old mail carrier at the time. He was in his sixties during the time, he and I did. Yeah.
Where did he live?

He lived at St. Claude between Duvain and St. Philip at the time. And he was the leader of one of the old onward bands. Best band from years back, putting in about eighteen hundred something. Way back.
Way back.
Way back. They taught me. And from there on, well, I organized a seven piece band.
Had you played any instrument before you took up some of them?
No, no, no, no, none at all.
Any even little whistles or guitar or anything? No, just taking a liking to the trumpet.
Just taking a liking to the trumpet. By being given to me, you see. That's what she said.
When you were young, did you hear some good trumpet players? Who did you like when you were a boy?
Oh, I always admired Louis playing. Always did. Louis.
When you were a boy, do you remember the parades you'd followed? Oh yeah. Who played those?
Joe Nicholas, we used to call Wooden Joe. Yeah. Celestan, all like that.
Do you remember?
The Eureka band. Yeah. Still up yet. I mean, some of the members yet. The old tuxedas. All of them I put in, knew the men, you know.
Do you remember Manuel Perez? Oh yeah.
In fact, I lived at home often with his sons, you know.
Did you ever play with Manuel Perez? No, I never worked with him any, no.
Never worked with him. No, I never worked with him. I knew the family well. Did you ever hear Joe Oliver?
No.
I never knew him.
Freddie Kepper, did you ever hear him? Yeah, the Kepper's brother, yeah.
There was one playing guitar. Louie Kepper. Louie, yeah, I know him personally, yes. I know him.
Do you remember your very first job that you played on the trumpet?
Playing with Arnold DePass, he's not deceased. He was an old time drummer too, an old drummer.
Yes, I've heard of him.

He used to play those fraternity dances at any time all along St. Charles Avenue. You know, and you get all those fraternities, different organizations. And that's how I began to play out, like one job to another.
Do you remember who else was in those bands? No. That early band, Arnold DePox?

There's a, let me see, a guy which is called Bill Phillips, drummer. I don't know if he's working anymore, if he's still living. You see that drummer. I heard the door. I don't know if he's in sax. Oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh. Don't you remember when you work with Billy? The old man, he smoked him in cigarettes.
Oh, oh, oh, oh. George Stewart. Huh?
George Stewart.
George Stewart. What did he play?

Clarinet? Sax. Sax. Most of the clarinet in that time, but he played a little sax too also. That George Stewart. I don't know if he's still living yet. I don't know. And one of the Dave, like Johnny Dave, banjo. Oh, yeah.
Who else?
There was a Cobet tour, a Reese Cobet. I don't know if he's in this city, he left four years ago too. Fat fella, saxophone player too. Cobet.
Yeah. Well, another trumpet I was going to ask you about, did you hear of Bunk Johnson ever when you were young?
No, not when I was young. I heard him years after though. I met him in Lake Charles, recently, yeah.
Do you remember who he was playing with or what?
At the time he was playing with, well, I know one of them then. That was a brother like Chiney. Chiney, what he was called Chiney with a drummer with Celeste Ant one time.
Oh, yes. Foster, I guess.
Foster, Foster, yeah. Abbey Foster, yes. And he was with Bunk then? Yeah, he was with Bunk Johnson then. Oh, yeah. At that time.
How did Bunk play then?
Oh, played swell. Did he? He was known as, you know, good drummer play at the time.
Yeah. Did he have, he didn't have false teeth then? Did he have his own teeth then?
No, when I met him he had false teeth. He had false teeth?
Yeah, but he still was playing.

He was strong at the time. It's been about, I don't know, 15 years. Huh? It's been about 15 years. Oh, that's before you know I married, married 24 years. Yeah, yeah, I met him in a minute. I met him in a minute. Yes, we might put that.
When were you married? I was married, this is the 28th of March past, 24 years. 24 years ago.
Yeah, 24 years ago.
Well, I didn't know you then, when you were playing with Bunk in a minute. Oh, that's right, yeah.
When, you might tell a little bit about your life and give D.D. a rest. When you started in music, about your family, the, did your mother and father play any instruments?
Yes, pianos.
They all play piano. All of your sisters, I believe you told me before, played piano.

All played piano. All my niece's nephew plays piano. Everyone in the family is musical pianos. Yeah. Of course, they take other instruments that they wanted to learn. Some one is trombone, one is sax.
Yeah, sure.
Like that, and one banjo. But they still got that piano. They still got that piano.
How long did you live in your hometown before you moved away?
I lived in my hometown. I got it before I went away. I was around 15 years old when I left my hometown. And that's when I went out.
Where did you go then? Well, I started traveling. Just traveling and playing music then?

Yeah, I was playing music. Playing music, it sure was. Who taught you on piano? Did you have lessons on piano or pick it up? None of us never had no lessons. Just picked it up. From my mother and father, that's all. That's why I accumulated that, through my mother and father.
Did you have any book when you learned or just play by ear?

Just play by ear. Anything I heard I wanted to play, I just went on and played it. And the first thing I learned how to play, I couldn't hardly talk good. I wasn't big enough to hardly make good on the piano, you know, then, because I was quite small. It was the blues. I never did love but one man in my life, he was a married man, I'd taken him from his wife. I never forget that long as I lived. That's the first thing I thought I sang in the blues. And then by, growing up, my sister Edna and I, we decided we would go out and show business.
Did you explain that, were you about the third sister or how, were the others older, how many were older than you?
Well, Sadie older than you? Sadie and Edna older and I, see. And then comes me and then come Ida, Ida's the baby girls.
Did your father or mother ever play in any bands or? No, they never did.
They just played most around the church. Played church. Which church did they play?
What kind of a church? Was it Baptist or Methodist? Baptist. Baptist.
Which church did you belong to, D.D.? Catholic, all of them.
Yeah, Catholic, that's what I thought. Could you tell us some more about that show, you say you went and played with shows and all that?

Well, my sister Edna and I went out on the show business. And when we left home, I was about 15 years of age. And the first show we went on was what's called Mighty Wiggle, Mighty Wiggle Carnival. And it was owned by Jack Schaefer.
Where did they travel? Florida or?
Yeah, they traveled all over Florida and all in the South, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Tennessee, all up the lines. But I didn't go up the line with them. Yes, I see.
I see.

All down, Miami, Cedar Keys, Micah Nopi, Kendry, Orlando, O'Kellar, Wildwood, Tallahassee, Jacksonville, Daytona, Lakeland. Was that more like a carnival show? It was a carnival, it was a carnival, yeah. What did you play for? I was playing a pipe organ in the color ministry show. That's what I was playing. And Edna, she danced stage. Did you do any singing with it too? Yeah, I used to get up there, I used to, I used to, I used to, I used to, I used to double. Yeah.
I used to double.
Sing, dance too. When I get tired of playing, Edna, she was sitting, playing with the band. Like that, see.
Your sister was in the same show.
Yeah, she and I was in the, she and I was together.
Did she ever play with any bands or come to New Orleans?
Yeah, she was, she's been in several times, I mean, since I've been married to Didi.
She worked with me for a while up in French Quarters.
Oh, does she?
Yeah, years back. Four or five months she worked with me studying.
Yeah, she came here and I, you worked at the Cat and Phil. Cat and Phil, that's on. Right there on, on Dolphin and, uh,
Chant and Dolph.
Just block the side of what they call, used to call it a coconut rope, used to be the pig pen. Oh, sure, I remember that.
Yeah. Yeah, I remember. Once when, when Piku played there. Yeah, me and Piku worked there together. Yeah, yeah.
Me and Piku worked at the pig pen together.
Well, you might tell some of the early bands you played with when you left the, the shows. When did you come to New Orleans, Billy?

Well, I came to New Orleans and, I made it, my first trip to New Orleans, that's when my sister Sadie were here. She was playing on Steamer Madison Boat. That's when her and, uh, her first husband was together. Bebe Chani. Oh, yeah. Drummer. Well, she taken sick, well, I was, I was playing with the Nighthawk Orchestra band in Birmingham. So, after she told me she was sick, I left Birmingham and came to New Orleans. That's when my first trip. See? And, uh, well, I was, went to work on the boat in her place. So she was able to go back on the boat. Is that on the lake? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. On the lake. Well, I worked on the boat with Chani. Let me see if I can remember now Chani. Let me see if I can remember. I know Chani. Ruben and Oliver. Ruben was known when I went to, uh, with Sadie and Chani. Huh? No. That's when Ruby taken the boat after Sadie. You know what I'm saying? But Chani, that's when Sadie was living over on Allen Street. No, I didn't know that. Let me see Sadie. Let me see Chani. And they had a little bright fella there. They used to call him Derby. Just about, by a high gun. That's all they ever called him. He was. Derby?
Yeah. He played trumpet or what did he play?
He played, uh, he played sax.
Saxophone.

I just remember. Well, that's all right. Buddy P.T. Buddy P.T. was played. Oh, Buddy P.T. played over on the boat? Yeah, Buddy, yeah. On the boat, yeah. That's when it was Buddy. Buddy. That's the gang I played with today. But I didn't know him. I just met him by me coming on a trip down here. And then I stayed here until she got well. She went back on a boat. Then, uh, that's where I met Lawrence Toker. Lawrence. Lawrence come to get her. To get some musician for him to go over to Mandeville or somewhere over that, over the lake to play. You know? And I was, well, I was going to leave that Monday night going back to Birmingham. So by me being over, stayed over. So I stayed over and worked with Lawrence. Them, uh, few nights over the lake, you see. With them. Then I left, went on back to Birmingham to my band, you see.
I want to ask about that band in Birmingham. What was the name of it again?
Nighthawk Orchestra. Nighthawk.
Uh-huh. I remember some records made by some Birmingham bands. I think one was called Blackbirds of Paradise or something. Do you remember a band like that?
No, I don't remember.
Did you ever make any records over there?
No, I didn't make, no, I never made them. No, I didn't make the record. No, I didn't make the record at all.
Who was the leader of the band? Do you remember? I really don't forgot.
Been a long time, of course.
Been here. Long time. Another thing, I don't like to worry a lot about those old times. I like to hear about it.

I would make it to you. And then, uh, that's the band I played with in Birmingham. All right. I lived in Birmingham. I went down in Florida. I went home, you see. Then, I joined the band of Mac Merrimickles Band. See. I worked with them. See, well, most of all the fellas was in Florida, was out of Florida, except Mac. And also the trombone, he was out of Mobile with George, uh, George Morris. He was out of Mobile. Well, I worked with them. Long time. Just traveling around on the road, see. And then after I, uh, left for Mac Band, I worked with a band in Orlando. A fella named Joe People. That was his name, Joe People.
I'm wondering if you remember any of the early piano players over in Florida. Can you remember either men or women, aside from your own family? Who they were, how they played, what style of...
Oh, they played this old... Everyone that played was all my style of playing. It's like I play now. All jazz.
Mostly blues players, too?
All the jazz, jazz music.
Play much ragtime?

Yeah, plenty ragtime music. There was a girl named Willie Woods. Willie Woods. She was a great piano player. There was Florida Beck. She was a number one piano player. Was a woman? Yeah. Two women of course.
Both of them, they... Yeah. So, Miss Woods was a...
Yeah, Woods was a piano... And also Miss Beck.
Beck.
And also... Well, where did they work, those women?
Where would they work? In a band or did they work in the bar rooms?

They worked in different bands. Well, I mean, you know bands, but they ain't like theirs now, you see. Yeah, I understand. But they scattered around, you see. But most of them, most of them parties, see. People in the other days used to just have a party and hire piano players to play, you know, like that. Before the band thing got out, you know, like there, see. Then there's a girl right here now. I met Far Taken Sick. ! She named Josie. Josie. Yeah, Josie. She's living over the river. She's a little slender, bronze, can't go. She flipped some piano. Really? I see her use a team together, right. See?
I'd like to hear her. She's still here, isn't she?
Yeah, I met her. She was here. She lived over the river somewhere. She did tell me, but she told me that when she come over again that she was coming to see me.
Well, she still played piano, do you think?
She told me she, she told me she ain't playing no more.
She quit.

She quit. Yeah, she's playing in bands. She's playing in different bands like I was, see. And then, let's see. Nice band. Then another fella, he's there now, Joe Jesse. He was a trumpet player. He's from out of my hometown out of Florida. Yes. He was a great trumpet player. And also, a drummer called Teddy Bear in my hometown. Teddy Bear. He's, oh, he's there now, I guess. I'm not sure he's there now. There was, uh, the Douglas, Douglas, uh, Butts of Douglas. They had an orchestra. Big band. That's in Florida, Pensacola.

Mm-hmm. Well, can you tell us how did those bands compare with the, uh, well, when you came and played with Buddy Petit and heard some of the New Orleans bands, did they sound a good idea like the Florida bands or did they have a different swing to it? How did they sound?

Well, they all sounded all right to me. The same identical music because we saw swinging music, but the idea, just different faces. Yeah. It's different, you know, like a stranger come in. Well, she sure can play, he sure can play. That's it. Like it is right now. The music was the same, it's identical thing to me right then. You know, cause now, this Bebop stuff, I don't care, I don't use that, understand? But I'm just saying, well, that day, people was playing jazz. Yeah. Jazz, see, piano jazz, all that stuff.
But I wonder, did these Florida bands or the ones in Birmingham, did they sound about the same kind of, uh, Dixieland?

No, they sounded different. New Orleans style or different? No, different style all together. Different style, but they were playing jazz. But when the New Orleans, I don't know, New Orleans just had that regular swing. See, cause all them bands used to be in my hometown, and, uh, twice a week, different bands. They'd come over there. They would come with Buddy P.T. All Buddy P.T., did he come over there and play like this week, next week, because we had so many engaged, I mean places, but, um, we could put those bands. See? Yeah. Cause we had so many parks, see, and in the summertime, all our parks would be open up. See, we had parks on the water, bays, house, and everything like that, you see? Well, that's why he'll finish with music like that.
Did the people like those, uh, New Orleans bands better than the local?

They're still crazy about New Orleans bands. Uh-huh. They're still crazy about the music of New Orleans. And, uh, and then, uh, another fella, uh, this other fella was a great piano player I knew. That was, uh, uh, wait a minute, did he, what's Nelly Huston's name, Nelly Huston, I told you I knew him, you know? Charlie Seagher. Charlie Seagher, he was a great piano player. That was, uh, Nelly Lytton. Nelly Lytton, well I worked with us, you know, I worked with my band at one time.
Oh, I didn't know about him.

Yeah, well he got killed as a wreck. Yeah, yeah, yeah, you knew he was a trumpet band too. He was trumpet and piano, he was double trumpet and piano together. Oh, he was great. I never knew him. He came from Lake Charles, didn't he? That's right, that's where I formed a band in Lake Charles. Oh, Charlie Seagher, you know, Charlie Seagher, you know, he'd get, play trumpet with me and I'd play piano. Then he'd put the horn down, get on the piano, trumpet too and double ups. Double ups. Double ups, like that. That way he would work. Alternate, in other words. Alternate, just like that. Yeah.
Well, I played some good ones. We might ask D.D. a little bit more about some of his bands now.

I'll begin to play like a potato fraternity dances in two and all the bands. I'll go on all the paths and then I played with Ken Rene for it. He taught me a lot, you know. He'd get those what they call advertising on the trucks on the streets a long time ago and advertise, you know, stop at one corner, one band, play against the other. And if he'd get two jobs for the same day, we'd split the band, he'd give me so many men and he'd take so many and we'd play both engagements. I worked that way with Rene.
Excuse me, I was going to ask you more about when you first started on trumpet, if you had any real lessons or- No, when I first started, I just picked it up like that. You picked it up-
Then I went to Rene first, my first teacher, Kid Rene.
Did you ever take any lessons when they used a method book or anything?
Oh yes, I did. I used Otto Langley.
That was Mr. Scholle?
Oh yeah, strictly music, strictly music. In other words, he played several instruments, you see. More teaching than anything else.
But Rene didn't teach you out of a book or anything? No, no, no. Just show you out of a book.

By hearing finger into the trumpet. Starling, you know? And I worked with Rene, I worked with Buddy. You know, these bands at that time, when they were short of a man, well they'd hire, and if I was passable enough to hold a job they'd put them in their place or so. You understand? They'd get two jobs, they'd split up some of them men and send on a job with a would-be player, you understand? A beginner or something like that and break him in. That's the way that piece would work. In other words, they'd collect the biggest of the fee, you know how that works. Sure, yeah. You know, that's how that went, you know? And I played with many of them. Like all over the city, then in and out of town. Of course I worked in Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, when I was on the road with different organizations, bands we'd make up, play a job. That's a band in Florida. Go to Alabama, anywhere, and play a job.
Played in Pensacola, Florida.
Yes, so Billy has some pictures here to show us for a minute here. We'll look at them while we have them out.

Now, this one picture here. Yeah, it's made in Florida, my hometown. Billy on piano, and who are the other people? Now, this fella here, his home is in Milton, Florida. That's the sax, Alto Sax, I guess. Yeah, that's Charlie Pipson Sax, a great sax. And this fella over here, the drummer, he's an undertaker, he's a big undertaker in my hometown right now, R.A.D. R.A.D. He's like drums. That's what we had in Pensacola, Florida.
And who's the coronet? Is that D.D.?
That's D.D.

Oh, yeah, well, I thought I was going to say, I didn't know though he was in the Florida band. Yeah, yeah. I was going to say, it sure looks like D.D. I'm going to roll. Yeah, I'm going to roll. I'm going to roll. I didn't know what's wrong. He holds the horn like he does, and everything looks like D.D. When did you all get, I mean, I know when you got married, but when did you, how did you meet? I was going to ask about that. Influence, I was working with her sister Sadie.
Let me tell him how I met you. Let me tell him, because he ain't going to tell you that I got told you.

Maybe each one of you got a different story on that. Now, this is the case though. Well, see, when my sister went here Sadie, I was staying with Sadie, I was working around with Lawrence Togel and the different bands going around, you know, just wild, understand? Yeah. Just having my fun. And, I don't know, so I never did see the trouble. I might have seen him, but I wasn't paying no attention, really. I might have been in different places, you know, like we used to go out to what we call those speakeasers and things like that, you understand? I might have met him, might have been drinking with him before, I know of, you know, but I didn't know him personally, see? So finally one day Sadie was home, I was there, and D.D. came home. So I said to my sister, I just said, I just walked through and in, says hello, he says hello, and I'll come on, I'll go on again, see? That's all I have to say. So, when I came back home that evening, whenever they get back, I asked my sister, I says, Sadie, she said, huh? I said, who's that little fellow, just like that, who's that little fellow? She said, that's my trumpet player, trumpet player, I said, what's his name? Diddy, I said, Diddy, yeah? I said, huh, just like that. She said, did you know there's something I was going to say, you know? She said, what I was going to say? I said, that's your boyfriend? She said, no, that ain't no my boyfriend. She said, why you asked me something like that? I said, cause if it ain't your boyfriend, tell him I like the hell out of him. So, he said, listen, let me tell you one thing, say, nah, listen, Billy, I know you. He said, D.D. is a nice boy and everything, and Billy, I don't, you, I see for yourself, you don't mean no, no one man no good. I said, if I don't mean no one man no good, I sure hell mean him some good. Just like that.
No, no joke, sorry.

Now listen, I, alright. Now he was playing music with my sister. Uh-huh, yeah. See? And I was playing in another band, see? Oh, I bet you, yeah. See? Now he was working in one block, like this block, and I was working in the next block, on Decatur Street. So finally, I said, if you don't tell him I like him, I'm going to tell him myself. She said, well, you tell him. I'm sure I'm going to tell him. So my sister used to come and pick me up, you see, when she knocked off before I was, she'd come pick me up. Well, her and sometimes D.D. would come with her, you know, and sit down and play, you know, in my truck and play or play, see? Yeah. And I was having fun. Funny one night, D.D. came in there by herself to pick me up. She told him to come pick me up because she was feeling bad she was going in. Because I had to work about an hour later than she did. So I seen D.D. came in there, you know. D.D. said, Billy, Sadie told me to wait for you because she wasn't feeling too good she was going in. I said, okay. So, oh, that just made me feel good. I was going to walk home that morning. I wasn't going to catch no cab to go home. But D.D. catch a cab ride in, but I was going to walk in that morning. So, all right, so D.D. stayed there, shot knocked off. Band was all coming all together, you know. I think the other boys had to go that direction. Well, I come in my direction. So, maybe he come. We stopped in different places. We get us a little drink, you know. Come on. Get us a little drink. We walked on there. So I told D.D. I said, D.D. He said, huh. I said, listen, I said, did you get a message? He said, a message from who? He got very serious, you know. Yeah. He said, a message from who? I said, say, didn't tell you anything? He said, no, say, didn't tell me anything. He said, what you told Sady something to tell me? I said, yeah. He said, what did you tell Sady? I said, I told Sady to tell you I like the hell out of you. Then he said, shut up. I said, sure, I'm not kidding. Then he said, I been liking you, but I know how to get up that thing. Because every time he see me, I was riding with a bunch of fellas, you know, have my fun, you know. Let's have my fun. You know, what's that to tell us? You know, nothing like that. Then he said, you mean that? I said, shut up. I said, sure. Shut up, child. Yeah. Did he come pick me up every night, bring me home. I said, say, you go ahead home. I said, did he go bring me in. So, D and I, we must run together about three weeks. We decided to get married. So, when I told my sister Sady, I said, I'm going to get married. He said, married who? He said, who in the fool going to tell you crazy to marry something like you? I said, I said, me and Diddy go get married. She said, Billy, no, you ain't. I said, yes, I am too. She said, mm-mm. She said, well, I'm going to tell you one thing. She said, listen. She said, I'm going to tell you. Diddy is a fine fella. Diddy is a real sweet, nice fella. He's from a nice family, Billy. She said, I wouldn't want you to marry Diddy and make his life miserable. If you don't meet Diddy no good, I wouldn't advise you to marry. She said, because I know you. Just like that. She said, no, she didn't think I would ever settle down or anything. Because I was traveling to show and going all the time. I said, well, I made up my mind to settle down. I said, I find a man I love, I'm going to marry him. And from that day, to this day, D and I are still together. That's right. That's right.
We agreed.
That's it. Is that the right story, D, D?

Exactly. That's right. I know. I believe it. And believe me, from there on, we had a lot of fun. We'd tell them today. We'd tell them to enjoy a couple of one another. That's true. That's right. You've had a wonderful life together. Yeah, we have. We have experience. It's just one of those things and I'm excited, but still in all, I'll tell anybody I've got a wife. I will say that over again. That's right.
That's a long time. Longer than most marriages last.
And we're speaking with like all couples, now and then it's a little fuss, it don't mount anything. Oh sure. It's just one of those things, but we get along the two of us.
That's right.

Oh, I was crazy about that, she was getting behind me all the time, I'm going to Belmont Theater, that's why she worked at Belmont Theater in Pensacola, Florida. Yeah, indeed. Bessie was my regular, Bessie Smith was my regular blues song, she was.
Did you ever work on a show with her?
Bessie? Yeah, I did chorus work.
You did it in the chorus?
I did chorus work and I played piano.
I did it in the chorus. I did it in the chorus.

I did it in the chorus. See, Clarence William, Clarence William got sick, see, he couldn't work no more with her. And by me, I wasn't doing chorus, I could play piano right on, playing piano, that's why I got my style in the chorus, see. Like that.

Yeah, I wish I could have heard more of Bessie, I'm sorry I didn't hear Ma Rainey. Yeah. What kind of show did Ma Rainey travel with, do you remember when you'd hear what kind of a show it was, or what she did?
I forgot what, I forgot what, just but a vaudeville I saw like it, you know. Some kind of vaudeville. A vaudeville, yeah.
I didn't know if it was more like a carnival or minstrel shows or what kind of show she might have traveled with.

It was more carnival like, to my idea, now, it was more like a minister, see, because she had many chorus, chorus, girl dancing, more of a minister, like, you know. A lot of jokes and stuff. Yeah, two comedians, you know, like that, two comedians and a straight man with them, you see, and then the chorus girls, and she sang, you know, blues, you know.
Like that. Did you ever get to New Orleans when you were over here, or did you here in Florida and around the country?
Florida, that's where I first met her, Florida.
Where did you work with Bessie, where did their show, all over I suppose.

Yeah, I was in different towns, different spots, around Florida, you know. I never hit up the line, but I like that. You never got up the line? No, up the line. I never get up the line with none of those shows I worked with. Always stay down in my part of the country like that, when they go in my guitar. I just go home, you see, you know.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. So that time the show used to come to Pencil Court and get ready for a piano player at the Belmont Theatre. But people, they all, Mr. Cummings, he was the man that owned the Belmont Theatre, Cummings there. So we just said, all right, come on, Goodson. Gotta have one of y'all. Most glad to be my time, I'll be home all the time, I'll be ready to go. Just any one of the sisters, remember? Yeah, they come for one of the Goodson's, he didn't care which one they get, as long as you get to Goodson's play a show. Well they had a drummer there, he put in mind of, he's an old gentleman, then he put in mind of Joe Rene. He short and fat, big stomach, you know, and he'd sit down and play a drummer. But we used to get some kick out of it, Gus, I never would get over that, Gus, Nick, Gus, just kicks.

Rene had a style of drummer, his brother though, a drummer. The snare drummer would sit up like this one. That's what he played. Yeah. If he's sitting down like I'm sitting here, that's why he played the snare drum up here. And his hands were up. He played on those parades and put those drums up. That's why he played, sitting down. That was his style of playing. That kid Rene's brother.
I heard him on the record, never did see him, I wouldn't work from him. He's a fine fella, he's all right.

I got along with him, I'm not speaking. He's still living, isn't he? No, he died. Joe? Yeah. Joe died, ooh, Joe died, yeah. Both of them were? Seven years back, yeah, both then. Well I guess I knew it. Joe died after, after, after, after, in here, in here.
I thought, I was thinking Joe was still living.
No, no, no, Joe died, no. In other words he's claiming tommene poison. Well I forgot of him, wasn't he? Yeah.
Did he die after his brother Henry?
Oh he died after Henry, yeah, from tommene poison, food, food poison.
I don't remember that.
That's what I was told. Yes, yes indeed. Put him down.
Never did see him, I heard that he. He was such a big eater.
Yeah, I heard you big eater.
I heard he joined church or something.

Yeah and all that, but he died from food poisoning they claim. Yeah. Did he give up that? When some food, if not, I ain't say it, but I mean it's truly the truth. Yeah. When food was dumped, put out on the dump. That's where he. Oh. Can stuff, and I believe he got a hold of that. Oh no. He died from, what they call, tomane poison, food poison. That's what I understood now. That's what they had said. He lived back that way sometime during that time.
Yes. Who were some of the other good drummers you worked with that you liked?
Well, like I said, the past, the first man I started with, he was a good drummer. The whole time, oh yeah, the whole time. He used overhead pedals at the time though.
Oh yes, I've heard of that. Yeah.
The only one I know. Then after that, everybody was drumming. I don't know.
Yes, a lot of them. There's so many of them.
I wondered about trombone players, if you had any favorite trombone players.
I like Henry's playing, Sonny Henry. I play, I have a big Ike, he died too.
Ike?
Ike, he talks in Heavisand. Is that Robinson? Yeah, Ike Robinson, yeah, yeah, yeah. Ike, yeah. I work with him a lot.
I was thinking he was living, when did he die?
He did, Ike, he did.

He said, I saw Ike's wife. Is he living? Yeah, she told me, yeah, Ike, listen. He's sickly, he's sickly. You remember? Wait, I tell you what happened. I went into Trimmy, to get something. I went to Trimmy to buy something for you. And I told you, I saw Ike's wife, told me she's still living in the same place. And I was sitting out on the step about a couple of weeks ago, she passed out there. Yeah, I think he's sick. I think he's sick. But she told me, no, Ike ain't dead. Ike ain't just a big and fat kid. I know, I know. I know, I know. He was so sickly there, you know. Yeah. But he didn't die, cause I asked her. She don't know him. No, he's still living in it. I don't know. He's still living in it, I don't know. He's passed, his wife passed here. And I was sitting outside there.
I don't know him at all. I must see him very soon, but I don't, I thought he was still living. I didn't know. I hope so. I didn't know, I hope so myself.

Yeah, I think he's still living, cause she told me, Ike, this is a big and fat, he don't get around. I believe she told me, my mistake, his eye is kind of bad on his sight. I believe that's what she told me.

What's the sign if I play nice, right? You play nice, right? You play nice, right? You play nice, right? You play nice, right? Yeah, sure. That boy played, that played somebody. That's the song that played sax. That's the song that played sax during the time I worked at St. Claude Street. That boy had his feet so bad there. Oh man, how you call me? Played trombone. I can't call his name. Trombone.
Is that the Cadillac or was it on St. Claude?
No, no, no. St. Claude, no. St. Claude. St. Bernard. St. Claude. St. Claude. St. Claude. St. Claude.

St. Claude. I can't call that man's name too. name right. He and Chippard lived almost in the sand block at one time. We'll run across the name someplace. I'm trying to say that but I know it's good. I know the boy's good. He's working with me. You? I can't call the boy's name. Just about a minute left on here. Can you think of anything else about your life you'd like to tell or the old bands that you've played with? Either one of you? I'm more clear than I've told you before. I think you've covered everything pretty well. Anything about your sisters though since I don't know them and may not see them, Billy? That you could tell? Sadie, who she played with? You said she played at Piku, different ones there.
She played with Tuxedo and Papa Celestan. She played with Papa Celestan and Buddy P.T. The one I know, she played with Ike Morgan. She played with them.
Well that's quite a few of them. Your other sister Edna that was older, did she play with bands here in town much?

Well she had no, no she didn't play. She just worked with Diddy and her and her husband. See, they just come over here for a visit. She traveled show business all the time. segments.title: Opening: Billie's name, sisters, birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Billie gives her married and maiden (Goodson) names, names her surviving sisters, and says she was born in Mariana, Florida, in 1907.

segments.title: De De's birth and learning trumpet from Kid Rene
segments.summary: De De gives his 1904 birth in New Orleans, says no one in his family played, and tells how a cousin's old trumpet, lessons from Kid Rene and reading lessons from an older teacher led to his own seven-piece band.

segments.title: Boyhood trumpet favorites, parades and Manuel Perez
segments.summary: De De recalls admiring Louis, following parades with Wooden Joe and Celestin, the Eureka band, and knowing Manuel Perez's family and the Keppards.

segments.title: First jobs with Arnold DePass fraternity dance bands
segments.summary: De De's first jobs were with drummer Arnold DePass playing fraternity dances on St. Charles Avenue; he names sidemen Bill Phillips, George Stewart, Johnny Dave and Reese Cobet.

segments.title: Meeting Bunk Johnson in Lake Charles
segments.summary: De De says he met Bunk Johnson years later in Lake Charles with a drummer named Foster; Bunk had false teeth but still played strongly.

segments.title: Billie's musical family, learning piano and first blues
segments.summary: Billie says her parents and sisters all played piano by ear, mostly in the Baptist church; she learned blues first and later decided with Edna to go into show business.

segments.title: Touring with the Mighty Wiggle Carnival at fifteen
segments.summary: Billie and sister Edna left home at about fifteen with a carnival owned by Jack Schaefer, playing pipe organ in a show while Edna danced, travelling through Florida and the South.

segments.title: Edna working with De De in New Orleans at the Cat and Fiddle and the pig pen
segments.summary: Edna visited New Orleans and worked with De De for some months in the French Quarter; Billie recalls the club on Dolphin and the old pig pen.

segments.title: First trip to New Orleans: Sadie's boat, Nighthawk Orchestra and Mac's band
segments.summary: Billie describes coming from Birmingham's Nighthawk Orchestra to fill in for sick Sadie on a lake steamer, meeting Buddy Petit and Lawrence Toca, then joining Mac Merrimickle's band and Joe People's in Orlando.

segments.chapter: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
segments.title: Early Florida piano players and ragtime
segments.summary: Billie names women pianists Willie Woods and Florida Beck, party-playing before bands, Josie in New Orleans, and Florida trumpeter Joe Jesse.

segments.chapter: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
segments.title: Florida and Birmingham bands compared with New Orleans style; Lake Charles band
segments.summary: Billie says Florida bands played jazz but with a different style from New Orleans, which Floridians loved, and recalls a trumpet-and-piano doubler from Lake Charles.

segments.chapter: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
segments.title: De De's teachers and filling in for Kid Rene's and Buddy Petit's bands
segments.summary: De De explains lessons with Kid Rene and a method-book teacher, and how bandleaders sent beginners out to fill jobs when they split a band between two engagements.

segments.chapter: Florida bands and New Orleans comparison
segments.title: Pictures of the Pensacola band
segments.summary: Billie shows a Pensacola photo with a sax, undertaker drummer and De De on cornet.

segments.title: Billie first notices De De and tells Sadie she likes him
segments.summary: Billie tells how she saw De De, Sadie's trumpet player, told Sadie she liked him, and finally told him herself walking home after work on Decatur Street.

segments.title: Billie tells De De herself on Decatur Street
segments.summary: Billie waits for the trumpeter to pick her up after work and tells him directly that she likes him.

segments.title: Deciding to marry; life together
segments.summary: After three weeks they decided to marry despite Sadie's doubts about Billie settling down; they describe 24 happy years always together.

segments.chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
segments.title: De De's band travels: Paul Barnes, Nellie Lutcher, Texas, and sitting in with Bunk
segments.summary: De De describes leaving with Paul Barnes and organizing a seven-piece band touring Louisiana and Texas, Nellie Lutcher as pianist, and sitting in with Bunk.

segments.chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
segments.title: Kid Rene and Buddy Petit compared
segments.summary: De De says Kid Rene was his favorite, a fast-fingered high-range player of a better class of music, while Buddy Petit played ballhouse blues.

segments.chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
segments.title: Chris Kelly the blues man, mutes and high-note trumpeters
segments.summary: De De describes Chris Kelly as strictly a blues man whose playing could start fights, his plunger and tin-can mutes, and Albert Glenny working with him and Rene. Asked about high-note men, De De names Louis DeMaine.

segments.chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
segments.title: When De De first heard Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: De De says he did not know Armstrong as a boy and remembers Celestin's parade bands from that time.

segments.chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
segments.title: Brass bands and the Jefferson City Buzzards at Mardi Gras
segments.summary: De De led the Jefferson City Buzzards for over fifteen years at Mardi Gras and otherwise mixed in as a hire for club parades.

segments.title: Photographs: Pensacola beach, hotel and Naval Station
segments.summary: Looking at postcards and photos, they place Sanders Beach, the St. Carlos Hotel and the Naval Station auditorium in Pensacola where they played.

segments.title: Photo of De De's band with the guitarist Emile Barnes
segments.summary: Garbled discussion of a Crawford photo of a band rehearsal, trying to name the guitar player and recall places around New Orleans.

segments.title: Pensacola station, Mariana, and the Bunky club job
segments.summary: They place Pensacola and Mariana and recall working at Bunky's nightclub out on Highway 71, around the late 1940s into the Korean War period.

segments.title: Family photos: sisters, New York and a grandfather who played flute
segments.summary: Billie shows pictures of her sisters Ida and Sadie, De De's mother and a niece; De De says his mother's father was an opera flutist.

segments.title: Years at Lutcher's and the decline of club work
segments.summary: They say they worked at Luthjen's about ten years, four nights a week down to two, as television, jukeboxes and new management hurt the place.

segments.title: Union membership and working outside the union
segments.summary: Luthjen's was an open-shop job; De De says he left the union after a month because the officers took the best jobs, and he did better on his own.

segments.title: Family pictures, Panama City and Florida relatives
segments.summary: Billie shows pictures of a nephew trombonist, relatives in Florida, a 1944 postcard from Panama City where they played, a Mexico card and a church.

segments.title: De De's trip toward Mexico while in Texas
segments.summary: De De says he never reached California but was heading to Mexico when his band split in Fort Worth after an uncle died in a Mexican mine.

segments.title: Picture of De De's family
segments.summary: They look at a photo of De De at about twelve with his parents, brother and sister; one of nine children.

segments.title: Manuel Perez's playing and lessons
segments.summary: De De recalls Manuel Perez as a powerful street trumpeter like Joe Nicholas, and says he got a few lessons at his house on Sundays.

segments.title: Favorite clarinetists: Picou and Big Eye Louis Nelson
segments.summary: De De liked Picou and worked with him a lot; he praises Big Eye Louis's tone, who also worked at Luthjen's.

segments.title: How De De and Billie got the job at Lutcher's
segments.summary: Billie explains how Melvin Frank hired them at Luthjen's, Edna Francis filled in for her piano, and De De took over the band and hired his wife.

segments.title: Favorite blues singers: Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey
segments.summary: Billie says Bessie Smith was her favorite, disliked Ida Cox and Sara Martin, and compares Ma Rainey's heavy voice, recalling first playing for Bessie.

segments.title: Working on Bessie Smith's show as chorus and pianist
segments.summary: Billie did chorus work and then played piano when Bessie's pianist Clarence Williams fell ill.

segments.title: Ma Rainey's show
segments.summary: Billie describes Ma Rainey's carnival-minstrel show with comedians and chorus girls, which she saw in Florida.

segments.title: Bessie's shows in Florida and the Belmont Theatre in Pensacola
segments.summary: Billie says she worked with Bessie around Florida, never up the line, and that the Belmont Theatre's owner would hire any Goodson sister as pianist.

segments.title: Joe Rene the drummer, his death, and other drummers
segments.summary: De De describes Kid Rene's brother's raised snare-drum style and his reported death from food poisoning, then other drummers.

segments.title: Trombonists: Sonny Henry and Ike Robinson
segments.summary: De De names favorite trombonists Sonny Henry and Ike Robinson; Billie reports Ike is alive but sickly.

segments.title: Closing: Billie's sister Sadie and other sisters
segments.summary: Billie says Sadie played with Tuxedo, Celestin, Buddy Petit and Ike Morgan, and that Edna and the younger sisters only visited New Orleans.
